offered. In a collectivist state, towards which we seem to be moving, full employment may even mean that people must work -at what they are told to work at, where they -are told to work, and at w-h-at hours -and wages.^
This release from the Department of Labour was the cause of much discussion and some alarm among those at the meeting of the Winnipeg labour council. It appears to many that the government subscribes -to these policies, or that this is the policy of the government, and I should like some clarification by the minister in that respect.

Let me say first, without equivocation, that this does not represent the policy of the government or my own personal opinion. When I was charged with responsibility for selective service on both the military and civilian sides I made this observation to this House of Commons, or words to this effect; that I hoped nothing I had to do would in any way damage the basic principles of freedom that have made the Canadian people what they are. No doubt hon. members have followed our actions with respect to selective service, and they will agree that we went about removing controls perhaps more quickly than any other department in the government. I believe in a free country; I believe that people suffer for their sins if they do the wrong thing. That is basic.
Getting back to this letter, may I tell- my hon. friend that I receive the information service from one of the other departments, I forget what it is just now, and sometimes see articles which are critical of myself. That is a government agency. In the Department of Labour we have an- information service from which editorial and newspaper comments from all sections of the press are sent to civil servants across the country. The article in question here came from the Ottawa Journal, When I speak about the basic principles of freedom, let me say that I know something: about Mr. MacNamara, or at least I should^ and he thinks exactly as I do in these matters. By that I mean he is a liberal mentally; I* do not know what his politics were before he-became a civil servant. I wish to say further,. - Mr. Chairman, that this nation can thank goodness for Arthur MacNamara. I do not care about your O.B.U. or W.C.T.U. or any of the rest of them; let them say what they will. I am not addressing this particularly to my hon. friend, of course; I am speaking in vigorous terms because I believe what I am saying-

I do not think the W.C.T.U. wotdd care much about it.

Well, you cannot tell; sometimes people do silly things, even the W.C.T.U., although I do not wish to cast any reflection upon them. I do not know much about them; I belong on the other side of the fence. But I do resent that attack on Mr. MacNamara, because I know something of the contribution he has made to the life of this country. I know something about his social outlook, naturally, too. No doubt this editorial did appear in the Ottawa Journal. I do not know what prompted it, but certainly neither the party of my hon, friend nor the party which is to his left, nor the official opposition nor the government of the day-
The party that were to his left.

I do not mean the party down in the corner. I stopped right there; I am not fooling myself about these things. None of these parties subscribe by one iota to any expression of opinion in any newspaper to the effect that we are inevitably drifting toward collectivism. For one thing, the Canadian people are not foolish. When it comes to freedom I know of no nation on earth that has a deeper regard for the basic principles of freedom that have made the British people what they are.

At this stage of the session I suppose it is too late to make a speech, which I regret; so that I shall content myself with asking the minister a few questions. I imagine we shall be back here in about two months and a half, and perhaps all we need be concerned about now is that provision is made for situations which may develop in that time. It is too late this session to discuss policy, unless we intend to stay here until after Christmas.
If the minister has the information I should be glad if he would give the committee the latest figures as to applications for employment; placements; the number of those placements which are permanent, by which I mean in occupations which will continue for a period of time and which are not seasonal; the number that are seasonal, together with the number unemployed at the date mentioned, that is the number for which no jobs were available. If the government has any policy for assisting provinces and municipalities where large-scale unemployment takes place, I should like to know what it is.

I am sorry we have not the figures respecting seasonal and other kinds of employment. As a matter of fact, it is only since the establishment of unemployment 
insurance that we have really gone into the statistical feature of the matter. I have before me some figures which I shall have, boiled down so as to give some indication of the number of vacancies.
Then, the hon. member asked as to any special arrangements with the provinces. At the present time we have none. However, as he knows, the matter is now under discussion, in connection with the '.dominion-provincial conference on reconstruction.
Figures which have been handed me just now show that unfilled vacancies at the present time total 88,845 while unplaced applicants number 184,523.

I am somewhat disturbed about the unemployment insurance commission, something in which, as a trade unionist for many years, I have been keenly interested. When the measure was introduced I supported it and, along with some other hon. members, most of whom are not in the chamber this afternoon, considered it in the special committee. I believe the feeling at that time was that the bill was not a bad one. At the close of the session I did my best to have the unemployment insurance measure accepted throughout the country. There was some resistance to it, although not very much.
The Unemployment Insurance Act makes provision for administration by three commissioners, the first of whom was to be the chairman, the second to be appointed after consultation with employers, and the third after consultation with trade union organizations. The business of the commission can be carried on only after the vote of a majority of that commission has been secured. At the present time, and for some months past, only one commissioner has been acting. I do not know when the employers' representative resigned, but I understand that it was some time early in the autumn. Then, the term for which the workers' representative was appointed ended in September. Obviously, since that time the commission must have been carrying on without legal authority. If a majority of the commission is required, then that would mean that two would have to be present. When only one is present, clearly it is not functioning properly.
There is a provision in the act which states that if a commissioner is absent, and is not in a position to perform his duties, a substitute may be appointed. ' This indicates that when the measure was drawn up there was an understanding that there should be a full board at all times. All cases which come before the board present two points of view, namely those of the employers and those of

Supply-Labour
the employees, both of whom are contributors under the act. If decisions are made without representatives from vthose two groups I suggest that the way is left open for all sorts of suspicion that things are not being done properly.
On what date did Mr. Mitchell resign, and when did Mr. Talon's term expire? How has the commission been carrying on since those dates?

The date of Mr. Mitchell's resignation is July 31, and Mr. Talon's term expired on September 23.
As the hon. member knows, when I was in charge of organizing selective service certain powers were turned over to me, namely the powers of direction of the employment service. That order in council is still in operation. Perhaps it is more necessary to-day than it was when we first tried to organize the civilian population for war purposes.
The question of filling vacancies on the commission is under consideration, and in due course after this long session is over, and when we have had some rest, the country will be informed as to the composition of the commission.

Did the order in council
provide that the minister could function without the unemployment insurance commission?
I do not recall having seen any order in council which made provision for disregarding the unemployment insurance commission. If such order in council was not passed, then in my opinion a general order in council does not give the minister the right to dispense with the services of the commission set up under an act of parliament, and to perform the functions of the commission himself. This is a serious matter.

In what may have been a state of righteous indignation the minister, speaking a short time ago, made use of certain letters some of which sounded familiar to me. I was wondering whether he used only a jumble of letters, or whether he intended those letters to represent any particular organization.

No; there was nothing
sinister in my mind at the time. I was simply reaching out for letters. In fact, I am not quite sure what the letters W.C.T.U. stand for-although I believe it is a temperance organization. However, I want it clearly understood that I was not casting any reflection on any organization.

The minister has said
that the strike at Windsor is the only labour
disturbance of major importance at the present time. That strike has been going on much too long and, in view of the fact that other strikes have been settled more rapidly it seems to me that, had the minister been willing to take the necessary steps, the Windsor strike might have been settled more quickly.
In a strike of this kind between thousands of workers and the owners of a wealthy organization the time element is an important one. The people of Windsor are learning that, to their sorrow, to-day. They are learning, too, that in the type of struggle they are having, in which they seek to establish and maintain certain basic rights-and I believe the minister will agree that they are basic rights, since they include the right of union security-delay assists the owners. The very existence of the workers depends upon work. They are learning the truth of the assertion that those who own the machinery of production own their very way of living, their very lives. If the workers have no control over union security they are entirely at the mercy of those who hire and fire them.
It would appear to me that the delay has been much too long. Whether we say we are taking one side or the other does not make very much difference if the delay works to the disadvantage of one side or the other. The minister has stated several times that this strike is the responsibility of the province, that the province must deal with it. Apparently that was not the attitude taken in connection with other strikes. I remember the threatened strike in the packing industry when the department went ahead and appointed a controller and the matter was settled very quickly.
I should like to know if at the coming conference between the provinces and the dominion the government is going to make definite representations to bring about a decision as io whether these labour matters shall be left in the hands of the dominion or in the hands of the provinces. I think the federal government is right in trying to secure uniformity in these matters.
The Windsor strike is a very serious matter. It is a .most unfortunate thing to have happen during our reconversion period. Some decision should be made with regard to legislation, so that this could be settled. I am sure the house and Canada are waiting anxiously to know whether it is possible to reach some settlement in the near future without prejudicing the rights of these people for union security. Probably some mistakes have been made on both sides. I think the union has had some leadership that was in error. I suppose the choice of leadership was their own, but perhaps there was some blame on the other side.

So far as the management is concerned, they did come out with a statement: You pass legislation which grants to people union security, the same as they propose to do on the other side, and we will abide by it. You should not make us obey a certain rule and not make the rest of the manufacturers obey it. Set down your rules with regard to laboui and we will follow them, but what is good for us must be good for the other fellow. I think they were right in that regard.

What is wrong with that?

I do not know, but you will leam what is wrong with it. You will probably have to suffer for your sins. I know I would put the judgment of Mr. Phil Murray and Mr. William Green and Mr. John L. Lewis against the judgment of my hon. friend, and even myself, in connection with industrial matters.
Rackets.
My hon. friend says "rackets", but I do not think that is a fair thing to say about Mr. Phil Murray.
There can be union rackets.
I do not think that is a fair thing to say about Mr. Phil Murray. If my hon. friend had the same chivalry toward men in public life that Mr. Phil Murray has-
I did not say a word about Phil Murray.

I mentioned three men and the hon. member said something about rackets. However, that is beside the point; let us get on with the business. At the recent *conference on industrial ..matters with Mr. Truman it was made quite clear by the American Federation of Labor, the C.I.O. and the railroad brotherhoods that they did not * want even arbitration by law, let alone some of the things my hon. friend talks about. Do not forget when you put those things into force you are getting almost into that collective state at which my hon. friend and myself take offence; that is what will happen when the government says to a man, "This is the organization you have to belong to."
Not necessarily.

I know of what I speak; that is what it means. The dividing line between freedom and persecution is so thin that trade union leaders, the older trade union leaders, have shown that they have more sense than to talk about compulsion and coercion by law. They have reached a stage of maturity not as yet reached by the younger people who have not had so much experience. My hon. friend spoke about the Ford strike, but at the moment I am not going to say any more about it. I do not think it would be wise for me to do so.

The minister has been receiving a great deal of attention from different quarters and has been asked a number of questions about several things. I am neither going to give him advice nor ask him questions, I am just going to make two or three suggestions from one who is a layman. I am not an expert on labour matters. There are several members on this side who have been studying this question; they are not here at the moment and I do not want them to be blamed for what I am going to say.
First, I should like to refer to the comments the minister has just made. He said that we should thank goodness for Arthur MacNamara. I think he is putting that in the wrong way.
I think we should thank the province of Manitoba for letting him come here, and I think we should thank one of the outstanding governments of Manitoba for having trained him for twenty years before he came here.
The minister said something about the rules of this house. I believe that every hon, member will agree with what he has said. I suggest that he give the same speech to the cabinet the next time it meets, so that the changes he suggests may be approved and we can avoid these long hours and hurried discussions during the late days of the session.
I have three suggestions to make. The first is in connection with low wages paid in certain places. The second is in connection with wages in relation to shorter work weeks. The third concerns the controls that have been hampering men in seeking the work they desire.	[DOT]
I suggest first, that the wage freezing order be lifted or modified with respect to substandard wages. I know the minister will have an answer that perhaps satisfies him, that that can be done by application to certain of his labour boards and so on, but I suggest that at this time there should be a general lifting of that order in so far as those receiving sub-standard wages are concerned.
There are also some industries in provinces which now have a forty-eight hour week

Supply-Labour
regulation., as well as in other provinces, industries which are willing to give the same weekly wage for a forty-eight hour week as they now give for a fifty, fifty-two or fifty-four hour week. Government regulations now prevent that from being dlone. These men should not have to go through the present red tape to get that benefit. My third suggestion is that there be an abandonment of such controls as hamper men in seeking the work they desire. I do not intend to take more time with these suggestions. I am aware that many controls have been removed, and possibly more have been removed than we know of, but there are still some in effect that should be lifted.
I shall take just a couple of minutes more to amplify this suggestion. Wage control order P.C. 93S4, controls sub-standard as well as other wages. The freezing of those particular wages was widely protested. It does not do any good now to say that one doubted the wisdom of freezing wages that were below standard. We recognize that controls were necessary7 during the war and possibly could not be avoided, but now that the war is over, my suggestion is that the freezing orders affecting sub-standard wages should be lifted.
My second suggestion is with respect to the 48-hour week. Some of the provinces now provide for that. But there are industries employing men for fifty, fifty-two and fifty-four hours a week which are willing to pay them the same total weekly wage for a 48-hour week. My suggestion is that where industries are willing to do that, no regulation should prevent it from being done.
My third point is with respect to men seeking employment. Prior to the war, men were free to seek employment where they could find it and choose the work that suited them, but during the war regulations were imposed to place men in particular lines of employment. The war is now over. I recognize that, while many of our veterans are still away and for other reasons .perhaps, some regulation may still be necessary with respect to preventing men from seeking employment where they "can find it. Generally speaking, however, the sooner the regulations which hamper men from finding employment best suited to them are removed, the better.
I am not an expert on these matters, and if I have made any errors I trust the able officers-around the minister, will not point out to him that what I suggested should not be done.

The mind of the leader of the opposition I think travels veiy much along the same line as my own. The wage
control order is, at the moment, under review.
I would think, or I anticipate that the last vestige of selective service will disappear on the 1st of January. We still have the permit system left. We continued that for two reasons. One was to stop the drift from agriculture. We needed to keep the men in agriculture to get this year's crop out. They were given protection during the war because of the tremendous drift from agriculture into the armed services and into industry, and it was necessary to retain the permit system in order to get off the crop. The other reason was to permit us to give priority to veterans when vacancies occurred in industry and commerce.

The minister did not reply to my question whether the department was taking action at the dominion-provincial conference to establish a national labour code of uniform procedure dealing with labour disputes.	'
We have one now.
I mean establishing it on a solid basis.

I understand the implication of my hon. friend's question, but, as he knows, we have a constitution in this country known as the British North America Act which gives jurisdiction in these matters to the provinces. The only way in which this government or any other federal government in power can assume responsibility for a national code such as he has in mind is by amendment of the British North America Act. You cannot do it by agreement. You cannot break the law by agreement, as my legal friends will appreciate. I would think we should get back to free collective bargaining in the not too distant future. Then, of course, the constitutional rights enjoyed by the provinces will be assumed by them.

Is the department
making representations in this regard to the dominion-provincial conference?
We are discussing it and have discussed it at the conference.

I shall be glad to do
that. Will my hon. friend send it with a covering letter?

I will send it across the room to the minister now.
['Mr. Stewart.]

Let me give the minister an instance of the difficulties in which men are placed by the present controls. A man in my own part of the province, fifty-eight years of age, being unemployed, wrote to a packing company in Moose Jaw to find out whether they had the type of work he could do. A man of that age is not capable of doing very heavy work such as carrying around quarters of beef, but there is a certain type of work that he can do. The employment manager of Swift Canadian said that they had such employment for him but that he would have to get permission to go there from his local employment officer. This man interviewed his local officer and said that he had- employment in Moose Jaw and would like to get a permit to go. The chap in charge of the Yorkton office said, "Did you get a permit from us to go? Did you ask permission of us to write to this man?" He said. "No". The official said. "Well, we are giving you no permit; you do not go." The man said, "I would like to get work here but I could not find any." That man was compelled to go through the whole winter of 1944-45 looking for work. In the spring of the year he was unemployed, but he went around digging gardens and doing one thing and another. On the 5th of June the following year he received a sort of mimeographed letter. It came in with the rest of the mail and he thought it was of no particular consequence, but it was in actual fact a directive telling him that he was to go from Yorkton to the Swift Canadian company and take employment there. By this time he had established himself. He was working in the summertime at home, and he was satisfied with conditions. He thought this was merely a permit informing him that he could go if he wanted to; he did not understand its significance.
Was this man a farmer?

No, he was not. He works on a farm in the summertime, and he threshes in the fall. He works in the spring, and in the wintertime likes to get employment such as in the packing plant. He went on getting a living at small jobs around town in June and July, went out threshing in August, came 'back the first of September, and was met by a police officer who handed him a summons for not having obeyed the directive. He appeared at the police court and was fined some $55 for disobeying the directive. The man was absolutely innocent; he had asked for work, and had been constantly refused by the local officers. Then, receiving this letter and not recognizing that it was a directive,

Supply-Labour
he went on with his employment and was penalized in court to the extent of $50 and costs. That sort of thing has a serious effect on the attitude of some people toward the government.
The other case relates to unemployment insurance and will be brought up under the appropriate item. I bring this matter to the attention of the minister with a suggestion that when these directives are given the man should be notified of the seriousness of the offence in case he fails to obey, because this man was quite innocent of any intention of disobeying the law, and in view of the fact that he had been refused permission when he , needed work he did not think the notice he afterwards received meant anything more than that he could go to this job if he wanted to.

I think it can be said that in my department we act with expedition on receiving information of cases like that to which my hon. friend refers; and if I might say this in a kindly way, I think that is better than to bring such cases up on the floor of the House of Commons. I suggest that the telephone is the right way to get answers to a lot of questions which are asked in this chamber. I have been told that it costs $60 a minute to run the House of Commons. If a member rises to make general suggestions on policy or present basic principles, that is different. If my hon. friend will turn this case over to our department, even at this late date, with the other case he has, I will endeavour to see that the men obtain justice.

Could the minister give us any idea whether this plan will start again next year or in some predictable future time?

400,000	people. I
should like to point out that what was done in one place was to take a great number of young teachers and bring them together for a month to study together citizenship and life. It was a profitable experiment for the countiy.

have everyone, even members of parliament, under unemployment insurance. I think it is absolutely sound. Of course, in operating a big administrative machine like this you have to learn, and it takes time to develop so large an organization. The British scheme started oif with seven trades. We started off, I think, with between sixty-and seventy per cent of the people engaged in industry in this country. But I agree with my hon. friend that the quicker we can expand it to cover everybody, the better it will be for this dominion.
As to the figures the hon. member was asking for, live claims in October were 61,563; number of insured, two and three-quarter million.
Would the minister include women under the statement he has just made in respect of unemployment insurance?
They are already under the act.
What balance has the government in hand at the present time?
It is over $300 million.

I should like a short explanation from the minister of the item under administration of Unemployment Insurance Act for temporary assistance; it is somewhere in the neighbourhood of $10,668,000 as compared with a little over one million dollars for the permanent staff. There must be some special reason for the apparent disproportion of temporary to permanent staff. Could we have a brief explanation for the benefit of one who is not so familiar as the minister with the workings of the staff?

My hon. friend will appreciate that the unemployment insurance commission was set up during the war, and of course men who have served overseas have a priority in appointments to the civil service. That is basic law. For that reason the great majority of the people employed by the commission are on a temporary basis. That is in keeping with the law.
Is the situation such that this $10,000,000 or any large proportion of it will become a permanent payroll?
Yes. I am thinking ahead of my hon. friend.

May I ask the minister what he expects will be the financial results of the Hudson Bay railway project; not just the estimate for the present year, which is rapidly coming to a close, but what he expects will be the financial results for the next four or seven year period? I understand that during the brief hearing we had, while the manager was before the railways and shipping committee, it was pointed out that many of the structures and the right of way of the Hudson Bay railway were getting old, and that inasmuch as this railway does not set up any depreciation fund it is necessary to look after these rentals when they occur, so that obviously when the railway is new the rentals are not very costly, whereas, when the railway gets older, they mount up. Will the minister throw some light on anticipations for the next few years?

The position of the Hudson Bay railway is pretty much the same this year as it was last year. There is a decrease of $64,940 in the deficit and the amount of operating revenues has increased slightly this year as compared with last year, while operating expenses have also increased. I doubt whether any good purpose would be served by going into this matter at any length, because, as the hon. member knows, the manager of the Hudson Bay railway was here during the sitting of the railways and shipping committee and he gave evidence. I was under the impression then that the committee had obtained from him practically all the information that was desired at the time.

With reference to the Hudson Bay railway, I went to the report of the committee, on the recommendation of the minister the other evening, to find out what was contained in that report, because it had slipped by me the last couple of weeks, and while it contains a logical enough explanation for the figures that are before the committee, I consider that we should have a statement from the minister so that in some way we can tie up the future of the Hudson Bay railway with the port of Churchill and the northeast gateway of the prairies. It is thirty-six years now since we started building what we look upon as a more or less natural gateway into and out of the prairies. Because the weight of the House of Commons and of the people of Canada generally is away from that section of the world, those of us who believe that we can improve our economy by making use of the

Supply-Transport
facilities which are at our door, imperfect though they may be in part, believe that we have had neither a complete and fair report on the possibilities of that harbour nor a recent note of optimism from the department as to what we can do with respect to that northeast gateway. Must we just forget about it and consider it a dream, or can the minister give us a constructive hope, shall we say, that "there's gold in them thar waters up there?"
Ice anyway.

I went into this whole subject at great length on the discussion of the resolution of the hon, member for Churchill, and at that time I put on Hansard a number of tables and statements having to do with the capital cost of construction of the railway, of the harbour and other matters which I thought were of interest to the house. Apart from that there was the statement made by the manager of the railway before the railways and shipping committee. I can tell the hon. gentleman generally that the railway is being operated as efficiently as it possibly can be, and it is being operated by the Canadian National as agents for the Department of Transport.

That is not what I am getting at. I am not disputing the efficiency of the railway; I am thinking of the future success of that route. We feel in the west that it has not had a chance. I read the report of the committee, and I saw nothing in there that would indicate that the government is going to change its policy with respect to the disuse of the port of Churchill. Yet at the same time the minister himself refers to a resolution that was concurred in by a fairly handsome majority in this house during the session that is now closing. What is to be done?

The hon. gentleman asks me for a statement. I can only say that I have no other statement to make than that which I made on that occasion. If he wishes to know what the policy of the government is, it will depend on the amount of trade that can be taken out of that part of the country. The complaint thus far has been that there is' no ingoing cargo. There is wheat to be taken out of Churchill to other parts of the country and other parts of the world, but there is no ingoing cargo. That, as I say, has been the complaint. Hon. gentlemen opposite say: Well, if means were adopted to keep the port open for a longer period, perhaps something could be done. I do not disagree with that, but I say that, according to the experts of the Department of Transport, unfortunately the port can be kept open for 47696-2324
only a small portion of the year, and unless that position is changed I am afraid the outlook is not too bright. Again, something was said about assisting shipping interests to go into that port. In that regard I can say that the national harbours board and the Canadian shipping board have done a great deal in that direction, and are still working in an attempt to get grain out of Churchill. At this date I think it is too early to make any announcement about possible shipments in the spring.

I do not want this matter closed just yet. With regard to incoming cargoes, surely our trade commissioners in all parts of the world could arrange to have . cargoes brought to Churchill, just in the same way that they foster the promotion of international trade generally. This does not look to me at all like an insurmountable problem. Supposing we can operate Churchill for only three months, or for only four months. I do ' not believe either of these figures is given- by any official with finality, and if the government were sincere in operating the port of Churchill and the Hudson Bay route I suggest that it would use the facilities it already has all over the world in connection with bringing imports to this country. I should like the government to say that they will give this thing a trial for at least three or four years, using perhaps what is left of the Park Steamship company. Run it as a government proposition; let the government take the loss-that agrees with private enterprise principles anyway-and then if it should be profitable turn it over to private enterprise. If not, wash it out and we shall forget about it. We still think it is feasible.

I believe that point is well taken. As the matter stands to-day, the country is losing half a million dollars a year on the Hudson Bay railway, and seems destined to lose a great deal more as the line gets older. I bekeve, with the hon. member for Regina City, that the route should be given a fail trial. Now that the war is over, I believe the minister should see whether it will be possible to send enough grain shipments through Churchill, and perhaps get enough incoming shipments, to give the line a fair trial once and. for all, and let us discover whether we have a white elephant on our hands or whether the hopes of many people in the west are justified. Let us discover whether this line will at least carry itself, if not make a profit, and so take a burden off the taxpayers of this country. Could1 the minister say whether anything can be done by his department or by the government to give this line what

might be considered a fair trial in the opinion of those people who come from the west and who know something about the territory there?	.
I can add nothing to what I have said already.

Does the minister anticipate that this branch will again come under his jurisdiction as part of the Department of Transport, or will it remain in the other department?

Would the minister object if I made an observation on this item?

During the war many service personnel qualified in many aspects of air transport including pilotage, navigation, wireless operating, meteorology and all the other subjects which any aircrew member had to study. They have qualified under service regulations, but they are still forced by the Department of Transport to try examinations before they have the same privilege of operating aircraft under civil administration that ordinarily they would have under military administration. I refer particularly to their green licence cards which entitle them to fly blind over an airways route. All service pilots with any experience are qualified in the subjects which the Department of Transport now requires them to take in order to requalify for this licence. I have in mind the position in the United Kingdom, whereby the air ministry has control of the licensing of private and transport pilots; and any pilot or other aircrew category qualified under the military regulations is automatically given civil qualification. I should like to bring this point to {Mr. Jackman.]
the consideration of the minister, because even at the present time we have in the service men who are requalifying, wasting their time in studying subjects they have already taken.

897. Issue of radio receiving licences-(transport department only), $216,975.

Would the minister tell us exactly how much' it costs to collect the $4,018,000 in radio fees? I have never been able to get this straight. In the radio committee a year ago we were told that something like $230,000 was paid in vendors' commissions and $306,000 in administration costs. Is this $216,000 in addition to all that, as the cost of collecting some $4,000,000?

The total cost of collection of licence fees for the fiscal year 1944-45 is $217,348.60, and it is not included in the amount of fees received.

Supply-Transport

The way I figure it out is this: First of all, licence fees collected in those years, amounted to 84,018,000. Vendors' commissions amounted to $230,000, and there was an amount of $306,000 for administration fees. Then we have a further amount of $216,000 on top of that. If that is so, it means that it costs $753,000 to collect $4 million.
Why should we collect licence fees from those who own radios? Everybody listens to the radio and is interested in it. Why should the individual who owns the radio have to pay a nuisance tax of $2.50, when everyone in Canada gets the benefit of radio? The fact that it costs $753,000 to collect $4 million is simply ridiculous. What is the difficulty?
The total cost of the collection of fees is $521,472.75, which is made up of, first, commissions deducted at the source, amounting to $304,124.

I do not think that can be quite right. There is more involved in it than that. First of all, we have vendors' commissions of $230,000, as was explained in the radio committee, and administrative costs of $306,000. Where does this other figure come into the picture? Let us suppose we take only the first two items of $230,000 and $306,000-and these certainly are in the report .

we would have a total of $536,000 which it costs the country to collect $4 million. Why should anyone who owns a radio have to pay for that privilege, in these modem days when everyone enjoys the benefit of radio?
How much does it cost to investigate and to prosecute or to threaten prosecution in connection with those who do not buy their licences?

I can give the hon. member for St. Paul's the break-down, as I have it, of the cost of collecting radio licence fees. To the administration is charged $188,211 on account of the radio division and $29,136 on account of the treasury branch, making a total of $217,348.60. Then there are commissions deducted at the source, and not included in gross revenue, of $304,124.15, making a grand total of $521,472.75. That is the breakdown of the total cost.
What was the total amount of commissions collected from the public?
It amounts to $304,124.15.
And the total amount of revenue was $4 million?

The total revenue was $4,000,801.
An hon. MEMBER. Carried.
No, it is not carried yet.
I cannot give details as to the cost of investigations or prosecutions. Those figures are not kept separately, but I shall ask if they can be obtained.

We find that it costs $500,000 to collect $4 million. Does the minister not think that in the interests of economy it would be better to collect the money through the Department of National Revenue, and save that $500,000? Does the minister not think that each individual should contribute to radio, instead of limiting it to those who buy radios?

speechtext: I completely disagree with my hon. friend, because this is one of the finest form of occupation for those who have served their country in various ways in Canada. I would rather do it in some other way.

speechtext: You would.

I would rather do it in some other way. After all, we have to think about economy in this country. In 1938 we had 44,000 civil servants in Canada, and to-day we have 150,000. While in 1938 we paid $88 million for the conduct of oui civil service, to-day we pay $229 million. May I remind the government, which sits opposite, that we must think about economy in this country. That is why I have brought this matter up.

The Minister of Transport cannot set the rate.
Does the minister tell this committee that he has no authority over rates?
I said that the minister could not set the rate.
Does the minister mean by that, that the government cannot set the rate?
I will explain what I mean when I answer the hon. gentleman.

Then I do not know just where I stand in this matter. But no matter what rates are set on this ferry owned by the government of Canada, the government of Canada are in duty bound to fulfil their part of the contract and give us a rate which is in proportion to all the other rates on ferries for similar traffic. They are not giving us this rate now and we are the ones who are suffering. I have no complaint to make with reference to the Canadian National Railways. That is their business. If they can extract more money, that is for the benefit of themselves. Their service is all right; but their charge is prohibitive, and without any reason or satisfaction to the people of my province. Imagine a rate of $60.65 for carrying a truck a distance of eighteen miles! According to the transportation laws and the transportation commission which sat a few years ago in Ontario and established the rates for transportation by truck, this is a prohibitive rate to a great degree, and again I say to the minister that before another session of this house I want him to establish the rates on trucks. He may tell me and tell this committee that he has no authority to do that. I disagree, because his department and the government are the owners of this means of transport. I could say a great deal more with reference to these prohibitive rates on the car ferry, but I do not want to delay the committee.
Let me say, in closing, that we expect in our province at least fair treatment. It does not matter to the Canadian National Railways . whether the rate is $10.60 or whether it is $60.65, because every dollar that they lose in operating this ferry they bill the government for, and it is paid, and correctly so, according to the terms of agreement under which we entered into confederation. But I want to see
an individual who is operating a business so
protected by the new rates that he can deal with the maritime provinces of Nova Scotia and New Brunswick by truck traffic. I want the Minister of Transport to make a mental reservation regarding this matter and to provide us in the near future with a rate that is at least fair and equitable.

The hon. gentleman has raised a number of questions to which it would take some time to reply. I should like to reply at some length, but I feel that in justice and in fairness to the committee I should not go into any detail. But I wish to reply briefly to some of the questions he raised.
He said that the government should look after the transportation problems in Prince Edward Island. I say to him that the government has looked into those problems; is giving them serious consideration, and is spending a considerable sum of money. My hon. friend is not unmindful of the fact that already we have made commitments for improving the facilities at Tormentine and Borden.
That is under the Minister of Public Works.

It does not matter under whose department it is. At the moment it is under the Department of Transport, but that is aside from the question. We are spending on these facilities somewhere in the neighbourhood of $5,500,000. That is over and above the new ferry boat, which will cost between $4,500,000 and $5,000,000. That is over $11,000,000 for these facilities. So that I am sure the hon. gentleman cannot say that we are not looking with interest into the transportation problems between Prince Edward Island and the mainland.
He also asked with reference to the ferry boat. In my answer to his question on the order paper I stated that it would be late in the summer of 1946 before we could expect the ferry boat to be completed. speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
The leader of the opposition asked a question on Thursday last relating to external affairs, and I might give my hon. friend the answer immediately. He inquired whether the government had received an invitation from the United States government to attend an international trade conference. My hon, friend went on to inquire whether, if such an invitation should be received, the government would give favourable consideration to making its delegation to the proposed conference a non-partisan delegation rather than one representing only the government itself.
The position is that the United States government has proposed that the united nations

Supply-External Affairs
organization, once it is established, should take steps to convene a general international conference on trade and employment, if possible by the summer of 1946. The Canadian government has warmly welcomed the initiative which the United States government has taken in this matter and will give its full support in the united nations assembly to the proposal that such a conference be held. In the meantime I can only say that no consideration has yet been given to the composition of the Canadian delegation to such a conference.
I should like to take this opportunity of informing the committee that the government of Canada has accepted an invitation from the government of the United1 States to participate in a preliminary meeting, which will probably be held during the spring, to prepare concrete and concerted measures for the reduction of tariffs and other trade barriers, and generally to prepare the way for the successful accomplishment of the general objectives which we hope the united nations conference on trade and employment will be able to realize. I need not emphasize again the importance to Canada of restoring the world trading economy on the fullest and freest basis possible. No country has a greater stake in the attainment and consolidation of these objectives and we must be prepared to take our full part in cooperation with other like-minded nations in this great task.
Is the Prime Minister not making a general statement on this item?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I have not a prepared statement. I rather anticipated that a number of questions might be asked which I would seek to answer. In one way or another at different times during the session there have been extensive references to the more important matters of external affairs, and at this stage of the session I have not had an opportunity to prepare a statement of any length.

There are three questions I should like to place before the Prime Minister having to do with the Department of External Affairs. Before doing so, may I say that I consider it very unfortunate that the debate on external affairs should have come on so late in the session. The Prime Minister has been back from his trip to the United Kingdom and the United States for almost a month, and in the best interests of the country as well as of the house it would have been wiser for him to bring on this debate shortly after his return. The Canadian people have not had many opportunities over the last decade to consider foreign affairs. I think it
has been a weakness of this parliament that we have not had enough discussions on these topics, and as a result it has been difficult for public opinion to "crystallize. Then, of course, it is particularly unfortunate because so few members of parliament are here this week. Most of them have gone home, and only a comparative few will have had the privilege of listening to the discussions on external affairs which have token place to-day.
My first question has to do with Canada's position in the key negotiations which take place from time to time. For example, negotiations are now under way in Moscow, and there were similar negotiations in London in the early fall. They are of great importance. They may be settling the peace terms. In any event, there is no doubt that many of the terms will be settled at these conferences, which means that they may involve war oi peace in the future. Canada is very deeplj concerned with these negotiations, not onlj because of the part she has played in the recent war but also because of the part she undoubtedly would have to play in any future war, and more particularly because we are now one of the three trustees of atomic force. That has tremendously increased the responsibility of Canada 'as a nation in external affairs in the last year; I am confident the Prime Minister will agree with that statement. At this time the Canadian people are far more directly involved in the issues that have to be settled between the nations.
I suggest to the Prime Minister and to the committee that some procedure must be established so that Canada can take an active part in reaching these vital decisions. At the present time we are 'largely confined to complaining about the decisions after they have been reached and to trying to change them, which is a difficult thing to do. Once a decision is reached, it is almost impossible to make any far-reaching changes. The Prime Minister showed that this was Canada's position when he spoke in this house on September 27, referring to his projected visit to Europe. At page 491 of Hansard he said:
In this entire matter the understanding of the Canadian government, ias I have already intimated to the house, is that 'any draft treaty that results from the discussions of the council of foreign ministers will be of a preliminary character and that there will be an opportunity for Canada, as well as for other interested united nations, to express their views at a later stage.
It would be far more satisfactory if some method could be worked out whereby the Canadian house and the Canadian people could have additional knowledge of the facts and of the trends; have the time to consider them, and to hold discussions with the United
Supply-External Affairs

Kingdom and with other nations of the commonwealth, before decisions are reached. I have no doubt that something along that line is being done at the present time, under present practice; but it must go a great deal farther. I believe that Canada could get whatever procedure' she wished; that the United Kingdom and other nations of the commonwealth would follow our lead to a great extent if we suggested a change. So that, I repeat, my first question is for an explanation of Canada's position in respect of negotiations such as those being carried on at this time in Moscow.
My second question has to dio with Canada's policy in the Pacific. I would ask the Prime Minister to explain the attitude of his government toward Pacific affairs. That area has increased greatly in importance. In fact, I think the centre of world activity has now shifted from Europe, certainly to America and perhaps to the Pacific.
During the course of the war against Japan the United1 States did a great deal to open up areas in the Pacific. Russia has expanded and she is now taking an active interest in Manchuria; she is also very active in the northern part of the Pacific. China, of course, is like a giant just awakening from a long sleep. No one can tell what developments there may be on the mainland1 of Asia in the next decade or generation, but it is almost certain that they will be very great.
Then, Australia and New Zealand have developed remarkably during the war. They have taken a most aggressive position in Pacific affairs, and have told the rest of the world in no uncertain language just what they think their part should be in that area. What is Canada's policy on such questions as the allied advisory commission on Japan, which has been set up in Washington? Apparently the Russians wanted to have an allied control commission, functioning not in Washington but right in Tokyo. What position is Canada taking on that suggestion?
Are we in favour of a regional council for the Pacific? Some of the nations have been suggesting that there should be a council for that region, and Canada should take some position on the question. It is, of course, of vital interest to those Canadians who live on the Pacific slope. We should like to know what the Canadian government has in mind about a regional council for the Pacific. There is much to be said for such a council, because there are many problems which are peculiar to the Pacific area.
Then, what is Canada's policy with regard to a united nations trusteeship of the former

Japanese territories in the Pacific area? That, again, is a most important question; and we should like to know whether or not the government believes that such trusteeship should be established'.
My third question has to do with the work of the house itself in connection with external affairs. This year for the first time there was set up an external affairs committee. It is a very good committee, and the members who served on it took their work most seriously. On November 12, when the Prime Minister was away, that committee brought in a report, the last paragraph of which read as follows:
Your committee further recommends that it be empowered to consider matters connected with external affairs and report from time to time any suggestion or recommendation deemed advisable to the House of Commons.
That, of course, was a wide-open recommendation. The committee asked that it be given power to consider anything having to do with external affairs.
A few days later, on November 16, on a motion for concurrence, the Minister of Justice (Mr. St. Laurent) moved in amendment that the words "be now concurred in" at the end of the motion be struck out, and replaced by the following:
That the report be referred back to the said committee and that it have power to reconsider the recommendation expressed in the last paragraph of the report.
In moving that amendment, the Minister of Justice said that he thought the new committee had gone too far and had asked for powers that were much too wide. His suggestion was that they should consider only what was referred to them by the house.
In this matter there is a clear difference of opinion. Perhaps some middle ground can be found. May I suggest to the Prime Minister that the estimates for the Department of External Affairs might very well be referred to the external affairs committee. That is done now in respect of certain items in the Department of Transport which are referred to the special committee on government-owned railways and shipping. If this were done, if these estimates were referred, it would give the committee reasonable scope in the discussion of external affairs, and at the same time would not deprive the house of the right to discuss those estimates subsequently.
This new committee must not be crippled at the outset. There was great hope for it, in the speech of my leader when he proposed that it be set up, in the speech of the Prime Minister when he accepted the proposal, and in the speeches of the leaders of the other parties.

Supply-External Affairs
As I said at the opening of my remarks, matters connected with external affairs have not been, discussed at any great length in the Canadian parliament. However, they have become more and more important, until now there is nothing much more important which could be discussed either in committee or in the house. The standing committee could get at the various facts in connection with the estimates. It could call officials of the department, and could hear witnesses. It could help to keep the Department of External Affairs more closely in touch with the Canadian people. There would be valuable training for the members serving on the committee and the result would be to help the people of Canada to understand and to follow external affairs better than they do at the present time. Further, if my suggestions were followed it might be possible to reach unanimity on many questions connected with external affairs. So that I repeat my suggestion that the government adopt the policy of referring estimates of the department to the standing committee on external affairs at the beginning of the session.
Those are the three questions that I have to place before the Prime Minister to-night. It is impossible to overemphasize the importance of external affairs. Twice in twenty-five years young Canadians have sailed from our shores to fight, and in many cases to die, because of issues that arose beyond our boundaries. They have had to do that in order to prevent war from approaching our land. I believe that if the Canadian people are told the facts, if they are given an opportunity' to discuss and to understand the various issues, they will reach the right decision. But the leadership must come from the house itself. Therefore I suggest that in another session the Prime Minister see to it that more opportunity is given for a thorough examination of all questions having to do with external affairs.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, may I say to the hon. member for Vancouver South that I agree with practically all he has said this evening. Personally I am sorry that it was not possible to have these estimates brought down at an earlier time. I can give him an explanation which, however, he may regard as an excuse. The fact is that when I returned I found there was quite a lot to do. My hon. friend knows that part of the time was taken up with presiding at the dominion-provincial conference and studying questions in relation to it. He knows also that there were a number of very important measures which still had not been considered by the house, or if they had been considered, had
been considered only in one stage, and it was desired by the house to have them debated before anything else was taken up, or at least I so gathered. I met with the leaders of the three parties when I came back and we had a discussion as to how the business of the session should be arranged for the remainder of the session in order that we might get through about this time. In that discussion it was clearly emphasized that there were certain measures-for example, the emergency powers bill, the budget resolutions and other matters-which it was felt it was all-important should be dealt with by the house as soon as possible. I agreed to do all I could to see that those measures were brought forward as rapidly as possible. If I am not mistaken, I undertook to see that estimates which it might be requested should be brought down before others would be given priority. I do not recall any particular request that the estimates of external affairs should precede other estimates. I have been holding back, in part, to allow the business of the house to get along as rapidly as possible. I agree with my hon. friend that it is unfortunate that we should be discussing at this late stage of the session many matters that relate to external affairs.
I agree with my hon. friend that there is perhaps no more important phase of the government's work than that which relates to external affairs. I think he will agree that the importance of external affairs in the work of government has in Canada come to the fore very suddenly. During the period of the war there were strong reasons why we had to follow the course we did in regard to making our voice heard on many questions. I have said to the house that at times we found ourselves in an extremely embarrassing position. Decisions were being made by the Prime Minister of Great Britain associated with the President of the United States. Some of these decisions had to be made very quickly, and in a few instances we did not learn about them until after they had been made. But those cases were very few and there were good reasons for the haste that was required.
I had at that time to make up my mind whether I would protest each time we had been overlooked or whether I would look at the matter in a reasonable light and say, "Everything considered, as we are in a war, we had better allow this to pass without too much in the way of protest." But I can assure my hon. friend that there never was an occasion, while we may not have said much in the way of protest in public, that we did not place our position very strongly on record.
Coming to this present period, now that we are out of the war, I did as my hon. friend has
Supply-External Affairs

read from Hansard make a strong protest before I went across the Atlantic at Canada being invited to come for purposes of consultation on matters related to the settlement of the peace, and not invited to come as a principal,, to sit as such with others. One reason why I felt it important to go to England was to discuss that very phase of the situation with the prime minister and the minister of foreign affairs there. I thought that matters of the kind could be referred to much better in conversation than to be made an occasion for discussion across the Atlantic. I would say that I believe that the members of the British government have had and have every desire to see that Canada secures her full representation in important international negotiations, but to some extent the matter has been beyond their control.
My hon. friend has referred to the meeting of foreign ministers that took place in London. If I remember correctly, that meeting was the outgrowth of the conference held at Potsdam. Similarly, there is a conference taking place at Moscow to-day at which are present only the foreign ministers of the United Kingdom, the United States and the Soviet Union. That conference is the outcome of the decision reached at Yalta that the foreign ministers of the great powers involved in the war should meet every once in so often, I think it is every three or four months, to become-I do not say better acquainted with each other-better acquainted through conferring with one another, with all aspects of questions as they come up.
President Truman himself has said that he does not think there should be any more peace settlements by the great powers alone. In that connection I am sure the President was referring to a peace conference and the final settlement of peace terms. Canada has made her position very clearly known in that connection. In regard to matters that relate to the peace we expect to have all the powers recognize the great part which Canada played in this war, the great sacrifice of life that has been made, all that has contributed to victory on the part of our armed services, to say nothing of the much lesser but nevertheless very important contributions that Canada has made in the way of furnishing supplies, making loans, in fact giving assistance where it was needed without any consideration. We do expect and will expect that this country shall be given full recognition along with other powers that may have to do with these international matters that affect the future.
May I deal with the last subject to which my hon. friend referred before going on to the 
other two questions he asked? I think it would be all to the good to have the estimates of the Department of External Affairs referred to the committee on external affairs. That committee was formerly known as the committee on industrial and international relations, but its designation was changed at the beginning of this session. My impression is that 1 suggested at a previous session that we should refer the estimates of the Department of External Affairs to the committee on industrial and international relations. I know that I did advocate that course in regard to the estimates of different departments, namely,, that they should be referred to committees, and I did so for two reasons; first, in order that all members might be better informed on the work of the government in these matters and also because I believe it would involve a real saving in time in taking up the estimates themselves. I agree with my hon. friend that if the committee does go into these matters and takes up the estimates of any department-I am speaking now particularly of External Affairs-that should1 not preclude the fullest discussion on any of the items for external affairs when the report of the committee comes back to the house. I do think that the committee of supply might well decide that there are a large number of these-items which the standing committee had gone into so fully that there was no need of bringing them up again here and taking up the time of the house, but that it would rather pick out the items which it was felt should receive attention here.
The leader of the opposition also asked whether it was the intention to reappoint the committee on the revision of the rules of the house. I would answer him now by saying that that committee will certainly be reappointed. and I hope that it will consider very carefully how time can be saved in the House of Commons by a revision of the rules in some respects along the lines I have already suggested. The recommendation of the committee to which my hon. friend referred was that it be empowered to consider matters connected with external affairs and to report from time to time any suggestions or recommendations to the House of Commons. I think that was construed as being something very broadi and as rather a departure from the rules we follow generally in the house; namely, that when matters are referred to committees, they are referred to them specifically. For example, this committee on external affairs in its report referred to certain conventions they approved, and there were also the treaty of extradition and

Supply-External Affairs
one or two other matters which they considered. I think that is the right way in which to refer matters to a committee.
But with regard to External Affairs there is one very special reason why care must be taken as to the extent to which the committee might be authorized to go in investigating External Affairs generally. My hon. friend knows that in the Department of External Affairs there is a great deal of correspondence with different governments on matters that are under consideration and one thing above everything else that we have to watch is to see that where other governments are concerned their consent is obtained in advance of the disclosure of information that may be the subject of communication between those governments and our own. The committee might quite unconsciously, unless there was someone watching the situation pretty carefully, be going into some matters about which, if they were brought up in the House of Commons instead of in the committee the minister in charge would have to take responsibility. But I do not press that consideration too far. I think that what my hon. friend has in mind is that if the estimates as a whole were referred to a committee it could bring before it the officials of the External Affairs Department and if they had doubt as to the propriety to certain matters arising in the committee the matter could be considered and dealt with by the minister in the house. I am happy to join with my hon. friend in the move to have the estimates of External Affairs referred to the standing committee and I would hope that that committee might, as I have already suggested, bring down to a few topics the matters which subsequently need to be referred to in the House of Commons. Possibly later, when we call this particular resolution, and the amendment which has been proposed to refer the matter back for consideration the amendment might be allowed to pass as the committee will not be meeting again before another session.
My hon. friend asked me about Canada's position in certain key negotiations. I have touched on that to a limited extent. I cannot emphasize too strongly the right of this country to be one of the principals in any matters that have grown out of the war and relate to the making of the peace. I can assure him that we shall watch the situation carefully and press for our rights in that regard. 1
My hon. friend has made reference to Canada's policy in the Pacific. I had anticipated
that some questions would be asked in regard to the Pacific and I should like to answer his question as follows:
I should like to summarize briefly the situation with respect to the occupation and control of Japan. It will be recalled that, in October, Canada was invited to participate in the work of the far eastern advisory commission, a body convened in Washington to consider political matters connected with the fulfilment by Japan of its obligations under the instrument of surrender. The invitation was accepted, as the house was informed, and the Canadian ambassador in Washington was named as Canadian representative. A number of preliminary meetings have been held which have been chiefly devoted to examining the manifold problems with which the committee will have to deal and discussing the way in which its work can most profitably be arranged. The members taking part in these meetings, in addition to Canada, are the United Kingdom, the United States, China, Australia, France, India, the Philippine commonwealth, the Netherlands and New Zealand.
So far, the Soviet Union has not sent a representative to the commission, but it is my understanding that discussions are now proceeding between the four powers signatory to the Potsdam declaration -with a view to reconciling certain differences of opinion which have been expressed over methods of procedure. It is hoped that these discussions will result in the attendance of a Soviet representative, which will be genuinely welcomed by all.
It is premature as yet to attempt to predict, with any exactness, how the far eastern advisory commission will function and what role it will play. The important thing is that machinery has been created which will provide for joint discussions by all the nations directly concerned with the Pacific' of the intricate and far-reaching political problems occasioned by the defeat of Japan. An opportunity is thus afforded to the Canadian government to express its views on matters of concern to it and to share in the formulation of the policies that will be applied to Japan. I am hopeful that the far eastern advisory commission will make a worth-while contribution to the problem of creating conditions which will encourage the development by the Japanese people of a peaceful and democratic government.
Canada will be represented on the far eastern advisory commission during its forthcoming visit to Japan by Mr. E. H. Norman, a member of the external affairs service. Mr. Norman served at the Canadian legation in
Supply-External Affairs

Japan before the war and is a specialist in far eastern affairs. He will act in place of Mr. L. B. Pearson, the official Canadian representative on the commission, who will not be able to leave his post 'as Canadian ambassador in Washington for the time required for this visit to Japan.
Colonel L. M. Cosgrove of the trade commissioner service, has been appointed as economic consultant to the Canadian representative. Colonel Cosgrave served for many years as a trade commissioner in the far east, and has more recently been military attache at Canberra.
May I say a word with respect to China. The sense of relief experienced by all the united nations with the final surrender of Japan was surely nowhere felt more profoundly than in long-suffering China. To that great country it brought not only release from over eight years of war-indeed from fourteen years of continuous resistance-but a removal of the shadow of Japanese domination that had marked many more years of uncertainty and fear. We may well recall at this time the debt of gratitude the world owes to China for her resistance in those early days when she was willing to withstand the might of Japan. By a happy coincidence, on the very day when Japan signed the formal surrender terms in Tokyo bay, the Premier of China was the guest of our government, and as Prime Minister I was able to express to Dr. Soong Canada's congratulations and thanks, and to assure him of Canada's continued aid as China addressed herself to her tasks of reconstruction.
Canada with the other united nations looks with expectation and hope to China as she takes up her task of economic reconstruction and political development. Her leaders are fully aware that the task will not be without difficulties. News of recent days indicate a political condition yet unsettled and disturbed. At' this stage we can only affirm our confidence that the Chinese people will be able satisfactorily to solve their owm internal (problems. Good neighbours and far-off friends alike must be united in the hope that she may be completely successful in attaining the unity and strength that will enable her to take her place as a bulwark among the peace-loving and democratic nations of the world.
My hon. friend asks specifically with regard to the regional council in the Pacific. The government's policy has been to keep in touch with all these matters that relate to the Pacific as they have come up for consideration, but we have not thus far decided that it is advisable for us to become members of a regional council. It may be that the develop-

ments which will take place within the next short time will show the wisdom of Canada being a member of the regional council, but I think we have much to gain and nothing to lose by not taking too immediate a step in regard to what is most advisable in the intricate situation which exists at the present time in the Pacific.

I also asked the Prime
Minister the attitude of the government toward a united nations trusteeship of Japanese possessions.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: There is really nothing I can say at the present time about it, apd it is felt that it would be unwise to make any particular statement on that subject at the present time.

I have a few remarks to
make on a specific point and, .perhaps, a few questions to ask to which, I think, a great many people in Canada would like to get fairly specific answers from the Prime Minister. Before I do that, however, I wish to associate myself with the points made by the hon. member for Vancouver South in regard to the unsatisfactory condition in which we find ourselves with this Department of External Affairs; indeed, it applies also to a great many other departments. We have to go back to our homes without having an opportunity of getting information on many points which we would like to have clarified. Perhaps, however, the blame for this state of affairs does not rest with the government alone. It rests with the government for having failed to take the initiative in arranging the business of this house so that we can deal with matters with more satisfaction and more dispatch; but in my opinion, it must have the support of the opposition side of the house. I hope that when another session comes around, one of the first things we shall do will be so to arrange the work of the house that we shall deal more with practical matters rather than make speeches which in the end do not amount to anything anyway.
The Prime Minister said in another debate the other day that external affairs were of tremendous importance, that almost every subject we discussed to-day touches our affairs with other countries. I agree. May I say here that I was extremely glad when the Prime Minister found time earlier in the session- perhaps he did not find time; he just took it-to go to Great Britain and acquaint himself with many things at first hand. We criticize him, and we are going to continue to do so, but I admit that I felt somewhat relieved .when he took that trip, because I

Supply-External Affairs
considered at that time that international conditions were as bad as they could be without an eruption, and I believe to-day they are somewhat better. I hope that either the Prime Minister or whoever is in charge of external affairs *will find time in the future to visit other countries with which we have intimate international relations.
What I wish to touch on more specifically is a matter which was discussed in the session of 1944 under the estimates of the Department of External Affairs. I do not see any item concerning it in the estimates before me; but since this point was discussed and the Prime Minister made a very full statement on it at that time, I am going to bring it up to-night. I refer to the position of our citizens of Japanese origin. Their position has not been satisfactory to them and certainly not satisfactory, I think, to other Canadians, and now that we have come to the stage where the war is over, there must be some final solution in this important matter.
I am sure the Prime Minister has received communications from many organizations across Canada, organizations which are waiting to hear what he has to say on this subject. Had there been more time, I would have quoted at length from the Prime Minister's speech of August 4, 1944, with which in large measure I agree. The fault which I find with it is that that policy, in my opinion, has not been carried out. I will content myself with reading from part of the paragraph which appears on page 5916 of Hansard. The Prime Minister said:
Those who are disloyal must be removed. That is clear. Surely however it is not to be expected that the government will do yther than deal justly with those who are guilty of no crime, or even of any ill intention. For the government to act otherwise would ibe an acceptance of the standards of our enemies and the negation of the purposes for which we are fighting.
I agree with that whole-heartedly; it expresses my point of view absolutely. But I maintain that we have not dealt justly with these people, and it is for that reason that I wish the Prime Minister to-night, if he can, to give an assurance not only to these people themselves but to the people of Canada that democratic principles and the principles of freedom will be observed in our treatment of them. I should like to know if those who signed for repatriation and now wish to reconsider their signatures-
